claim: The histone chaperone Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 (CAF-1) deposits tetrameric (H3/H4)2 histones onto newly-synthesized DNA during DNA replication.
source: The histone chaperone Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 (CAF-1) deposits tetrameric (H3/H4)2 histones onto newly-synthesized DNA during DNA replication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of CAF-1, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Hydrogen/deuterium exchange and chemical cross-linking coupled to mass spectrometry reveal interactions that are essential for CAF-1 function in budding yeast.
source: Hydrogen/deuterium exchange and chemical cross-linking coupled to mass spectrometry reveal interactions that are essential for CAF-1 function in budding yeast
evidence: The manuscript describes HX and CX-MS experiments and validates findings with yeast functional assays (Figures 2C, 3C).

claim: The Cac1 subunit functions as a scaffold within the CAF-1-H3/H4 complex.
source: importantly indicate that the Cac1 subunit functions as a scaffold within the CAF-1-H3/H4 complex
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from HX and CX-MS data showing Cac1 interactions with all other subunits and histones (Figures 2, 3, 6).

claim: Cac1 alone binds H3/H4 with high affinity.
source: Cac1 alone not only binds H3/H4 with high affinity
evidence: Fluorescence anisotropy measurements show Cac1 binds H3/H4(Py) with KDapp = 97 nM (Figure 1B, Table 1).

claim: Cac1 promotes histone tetramerization independent of the other subunits.
source: Cac1 alone not only binds H3/H4 with high affinity, but also promotes histone tetramerization independent of the other subunits
evidence: EMSA and FRET assays demonstrate that Cac1 alone can tetramerize H3/H4 (Figure 1C, D).

claim: A minimal region in the C-terminus of Cac1, including the structured winged helix domain and glutamate/aspartate-rich domain, is sufficient to induce (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
source: Moreover, we identify a minimal region in the C-terminus of Cac1, including the structured winged helix domain and glutamate/aspartate-rich domain, which is sufficient to induce (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
evidence: Cac1386 (containing ED and WH domains) tetramerizes H3/H4 in EMSA and FRET assays, while shorter constructs do not (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Eukaryotic DNA is incorporated into chromatin structure via nucleosomes, which are units of ~146 DNA base pairs surrounding an octamer of histone proteins.
source: Eukaryotic DNA is incorporated into chromatin structure via nucleosomes, which are units of ~146 DNA base pairs surrounding an octamer of histone proteins (Kornberg, 1974).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Kornberg, 1974.

claim: The assembly and disassembly of nucleosomes is critical during DNA replication, as duplication of the genome requires concerted duplication of the resident histones.
source: The assembly and disassembly of nucleosomes is critical during DNA replication, as duplication of the genome requires concerted duplication of the resident histones.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Stillman, 1991 and general knowledge of chromatin replication.

claim: CAF-1 is intimately engaged in replication-dependent nucleosome assembly of nascent and parental histones H3/H4.
source: The CAF-1 (Chromatin Assembly Factor (1) histone chaperone is intimately engaged in replication-dependent nucleosome assembly of nascent (Verreault et al., 1996; Smith and Stillman, 1989; Tyler et al., 2001) and parental histones H3/H4
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Verreault et al., 1996; Smith and Stillman, 1989; Tyler et al., 2001).

claim: CAF-1 is recruited to the replication fork through PCNA (Proliferating cell nuclear antigen).
source: by way of recruitment to the replication fork through PCNA (Proliferating cell nuclear antigen) (Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Krawitz et al., 2002; Moggs et al., 2000; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Krawitz et al., 2002; Moggs et al., 2000; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2009).

claim: Parental H3/H4 histones are inherited in a conservative manner, in which intact (H3/H4)2 tetramers are partitioned onto the replicated daughter strands.
source: At the fork, parental H3/H4 histones are inherited in a conservative manner, in which intact (H3/H4)2 tetramers are partitioned onto the replicated daughter strands (Prior et al., 1980; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prior et al., 1980 and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: The monomeric form of CAF-1 tetramerizes H3/H4.
source: Multiple biophysical studies confirm that the monomeric form of CAF-1 tetramerizes H3/H4 (Winkler et al., 2012b; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Winkler et al., 2012b and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Asf1 binds one H3/H4 dimer.
source: Other monomeric chaperones such as Asf1 bind one H3/H4 dimer (English et al., 2005, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to English et al., 2005, 2006.

claim: Nap1, Vps75, Mcm2 and Rtt106 form homodimers and accommodate (H3/H4)2 tetramers.
source: whereas those that accommodate (H3/H4)2 tetramers – including Nap1, Vps75, Mcm2 and Rtt106 – form homodimers themselves (Bowman et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012; Hammond et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015; Richet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Bowman et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012; Hammond et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015; Richet et al., 2015).

claim: CAF-1 induces a unique mechanism of H3/H4 oligomerization.
source: Together, the evidence suggests that CAF-1 induces a unique mechanism of H3/H4 oligomerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with other chaperones that either bind dimers or form homodimers to bind tetramers.

claim: The budding yeast CAF-1 complex consists of subunits Cac1, Cac2, and Cac3.
source: The budding yeast CAF-1 complex consists of subunits Cac1, Cac2, and Cac3 (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GST-tagged Cac1, but not the other subunits, can co-immunoprecipitate endogenous human histones when expressed in HeLa cells.
source: GST-tagged Cac1, but not the other subunits, can co-immunoprecipitate endogenous human histones when expressed in HeLa cells (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: A single lysine to arginine substitution on H3 residue 56 abolished Cac1 binding.
source: A single lysine to arginine substitution on H3 residue 56 abolished Cac1 binding, implicating the first alpha helix (αN) in this interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work (Li et al., 2008).

claim: The H. sapiens and D. melanogaster homologs of Cac3 can bind H3/H4 with varying affinities.
source: Biophysical studies with the other subunits show that the H. sapiens and D. melanogaster homologs of Cac3 can bind H3/H4 with varying affinities (Song et al., 2008; Murzina et al., 2008; Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Song et al., 2008; Murzina et al., 2008; Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011).

claim: Dissociation constants for Cac1 and Cac2 binding to H3/H4 have not been reported.
source: However, dissociation constants for Cac1 and Cac2 binding to H3/H4 have not been reported
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: CAF-1 binds to H3/H4(Py) with low nanomolar affinity (KDapp = 5.3 nM).
source: Consistent with prior experiments, CAF-1 binds to H3/H4(Py) with low nanomolar affinity (KDapp = 5.3 nM) (Winkler et al., 2012b; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 1B, Table 1) and consistent with prior citations.

claim: Cac1 binds H3/H4 with sub-micromolar affinity (KDapp = 97 nM).
source: only Cac1 achieved saturable binding with sub-micromolar affinity for H3/H4 (KDapp = 97 nM)
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 1B, Table 1).

claim: Cac2 and Cac3 titrations did not reach saturation and displayed weak affinity for H3/H4.
source: Cac2 and Cac3 titrations, on the other hand, did not reach saturation and displayed weak affinity for H3/H4.
evidence: This is observed in fluorescence anisotropy experiments (Figure 1B, Table 1).

claim: Cac1 contributes substantially to H3/H4 binding.
source: These results suggest that Cac1 contributes substantially to H3/H4 binding
evidence: This is inferred from the binding affinity measurements showing Cac1 has much higher affinity than Cac2 or Cac3.

claim: The other subunits provide accessory interactions to promote a high-affinity CAF-1-H3/H4 complex.
source: and the other subunits provide accessory interactions to promote a high-affinity CAF-1-H3/H4 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that CAF-1 binds H3/H4 with higher affinity (5.3 nM) than Cac1 alone (97 nM).

claim: CAF-1 not only binds to H3/H4, but arranges the histones into a nucleosomal (H3/H4)2 tetramer.
source: Recent reports showed that CAF-1 not only binds to H3/H4, but arranges the histones into a nucleosomal (H3/H4)2 tetramer (Winkler et al., 2012b; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Winkler et al., 2012b and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Cac1 alone induces tetrasome formation.
source: Surprisingly, Cac1 alone induces tetrasome formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA (Figure 1C).

claim: Cac3 does not alter the basal fraction of tetrasomes formed.
source: In contrast, Cac3 does not alter the basal fraction of tetrasomes formed.
evidence: This is shown in the EMSA (Figure 1C).

claim: Cac2 induces more disome species.
source: Cac2 induces more disome species
evidence: This is shown in the EMSA (Figure 1C).

claim: The pre-formed Cac1/Cac2 complex deposits tetrasomes.
source: but the pre-formed Cac1/Cac2 complex deposits tetrasomes, suggesting that the Cac1 subunit promotes tetrasome assembly.
evidence: This is shown in the EMSA (Figure 1C).

claim: Cac1 induces FRET in H3/H4(CPM/FM) to a similar extent as CAF-1 or DNA.
source: but Cac1 increased the FRET signal of H3/H4(CPM/FM) to a similar extent as CAF-1 or DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET assay (Figure 1D).

claim: Neither Cac2 nor Cac3 induced FRET in H3/H4(CPM/FM).
source: Neither Cac2 nor Cac3 induced FRET
evidence: This is shown in the FRET assay (Figure 1D).

claim: Cac1 is sufficient for (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
source: Together, these data reveal that Cac1 is sufficient for (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
evidence: This is concluded from EMSA and FRET data (Figure 1C, D).

claim: Several regions of Cac1 show changes in HX upon binding H3/H4.
source: Several regions of Cac1 show changes in HX upon binding H3/H4.
evidence: This is shown in the HX-MS data (Figure 2A).

claim: The C-terminal half of Cac1 showed both increased HX (amino acids 550–591) and decreased HX (amino acids 304–322, 340–360, and 463–473) upon forming the CAF-1-H3/H4 complex.
source: In forming the CAF-1-H3/H4 complex, the C-terminal half of Cac1 showed both increased HX (amino acids 550–591) and decreased HX (amino acids 304–322, 340–360, and 463–473) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the HX-MS data (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The regions with decreased HX were candidates for potential protein-protein interactions between Cac1 and H3/H4.
source: The regions with decreased HX were candidates for potential protein-protein interactions between Cac1 and H3/H4 (Percy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a standard interpretation of HX data, supported by citation to Percy et al., 2012.

claim: The 304–322, 463–473 and 578–580 deletions in Cac1 compromised DNA damage resistance afforded by Cac1.
source: Of the strains that expressed Cac1 mutant proteins, the DNA damage resistance afforded by Cac1 was noticeably compromised by the 304–322, 463–473 and 578–580 deletions in Cac1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the yeast zeocin sensitivity assay (Figure 2C).

claim: The decreased HX in Cac1 regions 304–322, 463–473 and 578–580 upon H3/H4 binding likely reflects their importance for the physiological complex.
source: We conclude that the decreased HX in these regions upon H3/H4 binding likely reflects their importance for the physiological complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of HX data and yeast functional assays.

claim: The N-terminal loop and propeller blades 5 and 6 of Cac2 are protected from exchange following H3/H4 binding.
source: The HX data reveal that the N-terminal loop and propeller blades 5 and 6 are protected from exchange following H3/H4 binding (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the HX-MS data (Figure 2A and B).

claim: The Δ1–15, V273A/P275A/S276A/G277A, L316E/L318E, and Δ425–468 mutations in Cac2 displayed various degrees of sensitivity to zeocin-induced DNA damage.
source: Only the Δ1–15, V273A/P275A/S276A/G277A, L316E/L318E, and Δ425–468 mutations displayed various degrees of sensitivity to zeocin-induced DNA damage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the yeast zeocin sensitivity assay (Figure 2C).

claim: Cac2 regions at the N-terminus and in blade 6 identified in the HX analysis are functionally important in vivo.
source: From these data, we conclude that Cac2 regions at the N-terminus and in blade 6 identified in the HX analysis are functionally important in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of HX data and yeast functional assays.

claim: Cac3 exhibits little change in HX with H3/H4 association.
source: Cac3 exhibits little change in HX with H3/H4 association.
evidence: This is shown in the HX-MS data (Figure 2A and B).

claim: The HX data show no significant changes in deuteration in Cac3 when the CAF-1 complex is compared to CAF-1-H3/H4.
source: The HX data show no significant changes in deuteration in Cac3 when the CAF-1 complex is compared to CAF-1-H3/H4 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the HX-MS data (Figure 2A and B).

claim: H3/H4 binding to CAF-1 primarily promotes HX changes to Cac1 and Cac2, but not Cac3, in regions that are important for CAF-1 function in vivo.
source: Taken together, the HX and in vivo results indicate that H3/H4 binding to CAF-1 primarily promotes HX changes to Cac1 and Cac2, but not Cac3, in regions that are important for CAF-1 function in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of HX-MS data and yeast functional assays.

claim: Many intra-protein cross-links were observed in Cac1.
source: In addition to inter-subunit cross-links, many intra-protein cross-links were observed (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Intra-protein cross-links are especially prevalent in Cac1 within the first fifty amino acids, residues 118–334, and residues 460–593.
source: Such cross-links are especially prevalent in Cac1 within the first fifty amino acids, residues 118–334, and residues 460–593.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Intra-protein cross-links may reveal folded regions in Cac1, since unfolded, flexible domains likely cannot make stable cross-links.
source: These may reveal folded regions in Cac1, since unfolded, flexible domains likely cannot make stable cross-links (Leitner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-linking data, supported by citation to Leitner et al., 2010.

claim: Cross-links were observed between subunits Cac1 and Cac2, Cac1 and Cac3, but not between Cac2 and Cac3.
source: Within the CAF-1 and CAF-1-H3/H4 complexes, cross-links were observed between subunits Cac1 and Cac2, Cac1 and Cac3, but not between Cac2 and Cac3.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Cross-links between the Cac1 C-terminus to Cac2 are consistent with the last third of Cac1 binding to Cac2.
source: Cross-links between the Cac1 C-terminus to Cac2 (Figure 3A and B) are consistent with the last third of Cac1 binding to Cac2 (Kaufman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3A and B) and consistent with prior work (Kaufman et al., 1995).

claim: The Cac1 cross-links to Cac3 (Cac1K235 to Cac3K287 and Cac1K282 to Cac3K307) complement a prior observation in which a Cac1 L276P mutation abrogates binding to Cac3.
source: The Cac1 cross-links to Cac3 (Cac1K235 to Cac3K287 and Cac1K282 to Cac3K307) (Figure 3A and B) complement a prior observation in which a Cac1 L276P mutation abrogates binding to Cac3 (Krawitz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3A and B) and consistent with prior work (Krawitz et al., 2002).

claim: The Cac3 deletions ∆306–309 and ∆287–290 failed to rescue the DNA damage phenotype resulting from zeocin treatment.
source: Although wild type CAC3 rescued the DNA damage phenotype resulting from zeocin treatment, the deletions both failed to do so.
evidence: This is shown in the yeast zeocin sensitivity assay (Figure 3C).

claim: Cac3 residues 287–290 and 306–309 are important for CAF-1 structure and function.
source: This result suggests that these Cac3 residues are important for CAF-1 structure and function.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast functional assay (Figure 3C).

claim: Multiple residues within the Cac1 C-terminus (577–593) are proximal to both the H3 N-terminal tail lysines (4 and 18) and a C-terminal lysine 122.
source: Multiple residues within the Cac1 C-terminus (577–593) are proximal to both the H3 N-terminal tail lysines (4 and 18) and a C-terminal lysine 122.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: The predicted N-terminal helix of Cac3 cross-links to the H3 N-terminus.
source: The predicted N-terminal helix of Cac3 also cross-links to the H3 N-terminus.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: Cac1 lysines 444 and 577 cross-link to the αN and α1 helices of H3 (Cac1K444 to H3K64, Cac1K577 to H3K64, and Cac1K444 to H3E59).
source: Notably, Cac1 lysines 444 and 577 cross-link to the αN and α1 helices of H3 (Cac1K444 to H3K64, Cac1K577 to H3K64, and Cac1K444 to H3E59) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: Cac1 lysines 444 and 577 are close in space to H3-K56.
source: These residues are close in space to H3-K56 and reinforce reports that mutation or acetylation of H3-K56 alters binding to Cac1 (Winkler et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-linking data and supported by citations (Winkler et al., 2012b; Li et al., 2008).

claim: The C-terminal half of Cac1 is involved in cross-linking to histone H4.
source: The C-terminal half of Cac1 is also involved in cross-linking to histone H4.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: Cac1 residues 577–588 cross-link to the H4 N-terminal tail and to the core through H4K79.
source: Cac1 residues 577–588 cross-link to the H4 N-terminal tail and to the core through H4K79.
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: The H4 α2 helix cross-links to other Cac1 residues (H4E53 to Cac1K317 and H4K59 to Cac1E464).
source: K79 is immediately adjacent to the H4 α2 helix, which also cross-links to other Cac1 residues (H4E53 to Cac1K317 and H4K59 to Cac1E464) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: The Cac1 residues involved in histone cross-linking are located within peptides that exhibit significant changes in HX upon H3/H4 binding.
source: Importantly, the Cac1 residues involved in histone cross-linking are located within peptides that exhibit significant changes in HX upon H3/H4 binding (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing CX-MS data (Figure 3B) with HX-MS data (Figure 2A).

claim: Deletions of Cac1 residues 317 and 464 compromise CAF-1-dependent resistance to DNA damage in vivo.
source: Notably, these peptides include residues 317 and 464, the deletions of which compromise CAF-1-dependent resistance to DNA damage in vivo (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the yeast zeocin sensitivity assay (Figure 2C).

claim: The C-terminal half of Cac1 is involved in cross-links to both the tail and core domains of H3 and H4.
source: Thus, the C-terminal half of Cac1 is involved in cross-links to both the tail and core domains of H3 and H4.
evidence: This is concluded from the CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: Amino acids 386–606 within Cac1 are competent for histone tetramerization.
source: Both biophysical methods reveal that amino acids 386–606 within Cac1 are competent for histone tetramerization, whereas Cac1421 and Cac1457 are not.
evidence: This is shown by EMSA and FRET assays (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cac1421 and Cac1457 are not competent for histone tetramerization.
source: Both biophysical methods reveal that amino acids 386–606 within Cac1 are competent for histone tetramerization, whereas Cac1421 and Cac1457 are not.
evidence: This is shown by EMSA and FRET assays (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cac1 residues 386–457 may be responsible for a significant part of the binding interactions between Cac1 and H3/H4.
source: These results suggest that Cac1 residues 386–457 – which overlap much of the ED domain – may be responsible for a significant part of the binding interactions between Cac1 and H3/H4.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation experiments showing Cac1386 is sufficient but Cac1457 is not.

claim: Cac1386(Py) binds H3/H4 with KDapp = 210 nM.
source: In this assay, Cac1386(Py) binds H3/H4 (KDapp = 210 nM; Table 1) with a slightly weaker affinity than full-length Cac1 binding to H3/H4(Py) (KDapp = 97 nM).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 4C, Table 1).

claim: Cac1454(Py) binding to H3/H4 was significantly weaker than Cac1386(Py).
source: Cac1454(Py) binding to H3/H4, on the other hand, was significantly weaker (Table 1).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 4C, Table 1).

claim: Cac1386 binds H3/H4 and is sufficient to promote histone tetramerization.
source: Together, these data reveal that Cac1386 binds H3/H4 and is sufficient to promote histone tetramerization.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of binding and tetramerization assays (Figure 4A, B, C).

claim: Intact CAF-1 does not dimerize during the H3/H4 tetramerization process.
source: Although intact CAF-1 does not dimerize during the H3/H4 tetramerization process (Liu et al., 2012; Winkler et al., 2012b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012 and Winkler et al., 2012b.

claim: The H. sapiens and X. laevis homologs of the Cac1 subunit alone can dimerize in vivo through a sequence located C-terminal to the conserved ED domain.
source: previous work found that the H. sapiens and X. laevis homologs of the Cac1 subunit alone can dimerize in vivo through a sequence located C-terminal to the conserved ED domain (Quivy et al., 2001; Gérard et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quivy et al., 2001 and Gérard et al., 2006.

claim: Purified S. cerevisiae Cac1 elutes from size exclusion chromatography at a molecular weight consistent with a dimer.
source: Although this putative dimerization sequence is apparently not conserved in yeast, purified S. cerevisiae Cac1 elutes from size exclusion chromatography at a molecular weight consistent with a dimer, confirmed by multiangle light scattering (Winkler et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winkler et al., 2012b.

claim: The structure of Cac1457 was determined using molecular replacement to a resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: The structure was determined using molecular replacement to a resolution of 2.9 Å (Table 4) with coordinates from a recently determined structure of Cac1C (522–600) (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 4.

claim: Only amino acids 520–600 were visible in the electron density of the Cac1457 crystal structure.
source: Even though the entire 457–606 protein was present in the crystal (Figure 5A and data not shown), only amino acids 520–600 were visible in our electron density
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The 'wing' (576–581) of the Cac1 WH domain was disordered in the crystal structure.
source: and the 'wing' (576–581) was disordered.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The Cac1 WH domain structure is virtually identical to the reported Cac1C winged helix domain, with an overall root mean squared deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 1.14 Å for all atoms.
source: As expected, the structure we determined is virtually identical to the reported Cac1C winged helix (WH) domain, with an overall root mean squared deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 1.14 Å for all atoms (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: A crystallographic homo-dimer was observed for the Cac1 WH domain.
source: Indeed, we observed a crystallographic homo-dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Amino acids 572–600 form a symmetrical head-to-tail homo-dimerization interface that encompasses 651 Å2 of solvent-inaccessible surface area.
source: Amino acids 572–600 – corresponding to the last beta strand, loop, and alpha helix – form a symmetrical head-to-tail homo-dimerization interface (Figure 5A—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1D) that encompasses 651 Å2 of solvent-inaccessible surface area.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unlabeled Cac1386 titrated into Cac1386(Py) increased pyrene anisotropy with a dissociation constant of 26 nM in minimal buffer.
source: In a minimal buffer (M.B.), titration of unlabeled Cac1386 into Cac1386(Py) increased anisotropy with a dissociation constant of 26 nM (Figure 5B and Table 1).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 5B, Table 1).

claim: Unlabeled Cac1454 titrated into Cac1454(Py) increased pyrene anisotropy with a similar equilibrium constant (KD = 25 nM) in minimal buffer.
source: Likewise, unlabeled Cac1454 titrated into Cac1454(Py) increased pyrene anisotropy with a similar equilibrium constant (KD = 25 nM).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 5B, Table 1).

claim: The Cac1386(Py) - Cac1386 and Cac1454(Py) - Cac1454 dimers are destabilized by the histone buffer.
source: However, we also found that the Cac1386(Py) - Cac1386 and Cac1454(Py) - Cac1454 dimers are destabilized by the histone buffer (H.B.) that is typically used in H3/H4 equilibrium binding experiments (Donham et al., 2011; Scorgie et al., 2012; Karantza et al., 1996; Banks and Gloss, 2004; Winkler et al., 2012a; Winkler et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 5B) and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Monomeric Cac1386 is sufficient to tetramerize (H3/H4)2 but Cac1454 is not, even though both harbor the putative dimerization domain.
source: Importantly, our histone tetramerization assays performed in H.B. (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicate that monomeric Cac1386 is sufficient to tetramerize (H3/H4)2 but Cac1454 is not, even though both harbor the putative dimerization domain.
evidence: This is shown by EMSA and FRET assays (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cac1 dimerization is not necessary to promote (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
source: Therefore, Cac1 dimerization is not necessary to promote (H3/H4)2 tetramerization, consistent with the functional stoichiometry of CAF-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Cac1386 tetramerizes H3/H4 under conditions where it does not dimerize.

claim: The Cac1 C-terminus binds to DNA with a dissociation constant of ~2 µM.
source: In addition to H3/H4 binding, the Cac1 C-terminus has been reported to bind to DNA with a dissociation constant of ~2 µM (Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Cac1386(Py) directly binds Cac2 with a KD of 1.3 µM in histone buffer.
source: We also found that Cac1386(Py) directly binds Cac2 with a KD of 1.3 µM in H.B. (Figure 5C and Table 1).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 5C, Table 1).

claim: The Cac1 C-terminus has binding and conformational plasticity.
source: The weak binding of the Cac1 C-terminus to multiple partners, along with the histone-induced HX changes and simultaneous cross-links to both H3/H4 and Cac2, suggests that this region has binding and conformational plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of binding data, HX data, and CX-MS data.

claim: Binding of H3/H4 removes the excimer band in the Cac1386(Py) fluorescence spectrum.
source: We found that binding of H3/H4 removes this excimer band, whereas Cac2 does not change the spectrum.
evidence: This is shown by pyrene fluorescence spectroscopy (Figure 5D).

claim: Direct binding of H3/H4, but not Cac2, promotes a structural change in Cac1 near the ED domain.
source: These results indicate that direct binding of H3/H4, but not Cac2, promotes a structural change in Cac1 near the ED domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the pyrene fluorescence spectroscopy data (Figure 5D).

claim: Cac1 serves as a central scaffold with a modular architecture, which is subject to conformational changes upon H3/H4 binding.
source: Together, these results shape a functional model, wherein Cac1 serves as a central scaffold with a modular architecture, which is subject to conformational changes upon H3/H4 binding.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combination of HX, CX-MS, and biophysical data.

claim: CAF-1 primarily interacts with H3/H4 through the last third of Cac1.
source: CAF-1 primarily interacts with H3/H4 through the last third of Cac1 (Figures 3B and 6)
evidence: This is shown by CX-MS data (Figure 3B) and summarized in the model (Figure 6).

claim: The majority of Cac1-H3/H4 cross-links occur in the ED domain and the C-terminus to the cores and N-terminal tails of both H3 and H4.
source: with the majority of these Cac1-H3/H4 cross-links occurring in the ED domain and the C-terminus to the cores and N-terminal tails of both H3 and H4.
evidence: This is shown by CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: The Cac1-H3/H4 binding constant is more than an order of magnitude weaker than that of intact CAF-1.
source: However, the Cac1-H3/H4 binding constant is more than an order of magnitude weaker than that of intact CAF-1 (Winkler et al., 2012b; Liu et al., 2012) (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by comparing binding constants in Table 1 and supported by citations.

claim: The other subunits contribute to H3/H4 binding through direct interactions and possibly indirectly through interactions that stabilize Cac1.
source: Therefore, the other subunits contribute to H3/H4 binding through direct interactions as seen in the cross-linking study (Figure 3B), and also possibly indirectly through interactions that stabilize Cac1.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in binding affinities and the CX-MS data.

claim: CAF-1 co-purifies with specific post-translational modifications, namely H4 acetylated lysines 5, 8, 12, 16, and H3 acetylated lysine 56 and methylated (me1, me2, and me3) lysine 79.
source: CAF-1 is known to co-purify with specific post-translational modifications (PTMs), namely H4 acetylated lysines 5, 8, 12, 16, and H3 acetylated lysine 56 and methylated (me1, me2, and me3) lysine 79 (Zhou et al., 2006; Masumoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2006 and Masumoto et al., 2005.

claim: Mutations to the acetylatable lysines in H4 have a detrimental effect on CAF-1-dependent H3/H4 incorporation into chromatin.
source: Mutations to the acetylatable lysines in H4 have a detrimental effect on CAF-1-dependent H3/H4 incorporation into chromatin (Glowczewski et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glowczewski et al., 2004.

claim: A H3 K14R mutant decreases levels of bound Cac2 and has functional consequences in rDNA silencing and aging.
source: Moreover, a H3 K14R mutant, which cannot be acetylated, decreases levels of bound Cac2 and has functional consequences in rDNA silencing and aging (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of the H3 and H4 N-terminal tails did not alter CAF-1-H3/H4 binding affinity.
source: However, deletion of the H3 and H4 N-terminal tails did not alter CAF-1-H3/H4 binding affinity (Winkler et al., 2012b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winkler et al., 2012b.

claim: Deletion of the H3 and H4 N-terminal tails did not alter histone deposition by CAF-1.
source: nor histone deposition by CAF-1 (Shibahara et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shibahara et al., 2000.

claim: The cross-links from the H3/H4 tails to the WH domain are consistent with prior observations that tail deletions do not alter CAF-1 binding or deposition.
source: The cross-links from the H3/H4 tails to the WH domain, together with the weak Cac1454(Py) – H3/H4 affinity (Figures 3B, 4C and Table 1), are consistent with these prior observations.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of CX-MS data and binding data.

claim: The WH domain interacts with histone tails.
source: As the WH domain interacts with histone tails, our model reveals how histone N-terminal PTMs could modulate CAF-1 function in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the CX-MS data showing cross-links between the WH domain and histone tails.

claim: The core domains of both histone H3 and H4 cross-link to multiple regions in Cac1, including the middle domain, WH domain, and regions near the ED domain.
source: In contrast to the tails, the core domains of both histone H3 and H4 cross-link to multiple regions in Cac1, including the middle domain, WH domain, and regions near the ED domain.
evidence: This is shown by CX-MS data (Figure 3B).

claim: The cross-links in the vicinity of H3 K56 provide an explanation for the modulatory effect of H3 K56 acetylation on CAF-1 binding.
source: The cross-links in the vicinity of H3 K56 provide an explanation for the modulatory effect of H3 K56 acetylation on CAF-1 binding (Li et al., 2008; Winkler et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is inferred from the CX-MS data and supported by citations (Li et al., 2008; Winkler et al., 2012b).

claim: The direct cross-links of Cac1-Cac3 occur in a region near where Cac3 homologs from multi-cellular organisms bind helix α1 of H4.
source: The direct cross-links of Cac1-Cac3 occur in a region near where Cac3 homologs from multi-cellular organisms bind helix α1 of H4 (Nowak et al., 2011; Murzina et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the CX-MS data and supported by citations (Nowak et al., 2011; Murzina et al., 2008).

claim: Interactions previously observed between the H3 N-terminus with the top surface of the beta propeller do not coincide with any cross-links observed in this study.
source: However, interactions previously observed between the H3 N-terminus with the top surface of the beta propeller (Schmitges et al., 2011) do not coincide with any cross-links observed here.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of CX-MS data with prior work (Schmitges et al., 2011).

claim: The D. melanogaster homolog of Cac3 binds to the N-terminal peptides of either H3 or H4 with tight to modest affinity, respectively (KD = 35 nM for H4, KD = 2 µM for H3).
source: The D. melanogaster homolog of Cac3 binds to the N-terminal peptides of either H3 or H4 with tight to modest affinity, respectively (KD = 35 nM for H4, KD = 2 µM for H3) (Nowak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nowak et al., 2011.

claim: Yeast Cac3 might bind H3/H4 differently than other eukaryotic homologs.
source: That both of these interactions are tighter than our KD for Cac3 binding to H3/H4(Py) (Figure 1B) raises the possibility that yeast Cac3 might bind H3/H4 differently than other eukaryotic homologs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of binding affinities.

claim: The weak Cac2 and Cac3 interactions with histones measured here are consistent with the dearth of specific Cac2-H3/H4 and Cac3-H3/H4 cross-links.
source: The weak Cac2 and Cac3 interactions with histones measured here, together with the inability to tetramerize H3/H4, is consistent with the dearth of specific Cac2-H3/H4 and Cac3-H3/H4 cross-links.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of binding data and CX-MS data.

claim: The cross-links reported in this study are largely consistent with a recent report examining CAF-1 and CAF-1-H3/H4 cross-links.
source: Importantly, our cross-links are largely consistent with a recent report examining CAF-1 and CAF-1-H3/H4 cross-links (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with Kim et al., 2016.

claim: In both this study and Kim et al., the Cac1 middle domain cross-links to Cac2 and Cac3, and the Cac1 C-terminus cross-links to Cac2 and H3.
source: In both studies, the Cac1 middle domain cross-links to Cac2 and Cac3, and the Cac1 C-terminus cross-links to Cac2 and H3.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with Kim et al., 2016.

claim: This study reports an additional cross-link between the middle domain to H4 whereas Kim, et al. observe the middle domain cross-linking to H3.
source: We report an additional cross-link between the middle domain to H4 whereas Kim, et al. observe the middle domain cross-linking to H3
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with Kim et al., 2016.

claim: The electron microscopy data support the idea that Cac1 is a platform for interactions with Cac2, Cac3, and H3/H4.
source: The electron microscopy data also support the idea that Cac1 is a platform for these interactions, as Cac1 is physically associated with Cac2, Cac3, and H3/H4 (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2016.

claim: Chemical cross-linking is a capture method rather than an equilibrium one; thus, the abundance of cross-links is not suggestive of equilibrium binding constants.
source: Importantly, we emphasize that chemical cross-linking is a capture method rather than an equilibrium one; thus, the abundance of cross-links is not suggestive of equilibrium binding constants.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of cross-linking data.

claim: The bulk of the Cac1-H3/H4 interactions that contribute to lower the free energy of binding occur at the C-terminus of Cac1.
source: The bulk of the Cac1-H3/H4 interactions that contribute to lower the free energy of binding, therefore, indeed occur at the C-terminus of Cac1.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding affinity measurements showing Cac1386 binds H3/H4 with similar affinity to full-length Cac1.

claim: The Cac1 WH domain can form a homodimer.
source: Whereas the Cac1 WH domain can form a homodimer, this form is not required for (H3/H4)2 tetramerization (Figures 4A,B and 5A).
evidence: This is shown by crystal structure and fluorescence anisotropy (Figures 4A,B and 5A).

claim: The Cac1 WH domain homodimer form is not required for (H3/H4)2 tetramerization.
source: Whereas the Cac1 WH domain can form a homodimer, this form is not required for (H3/H4)2 tetramerization (Figures 4A,B and 5A).
evidence: This is shown by the fact that Cac1386 tetramerizes H3/H4 under conditions where it does not dimerize.

claim: The Cac1386 and Cac1454 monomer/dimer equilibrium can be significantly affected by changes in buffer composition.
source: The dimer form, however, was not observed in H.B. Thus, the Cac1386 and Cac1454 monomer/dimer equilibrium can be significantly affected by changes in buffer composition, similar to the H3/H4 dimer/tetramer forms (Donham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence anisotropy in different buffers (Figure 5B) and supported by citation.

claim: CAF-1 is a monomer in complex with H3/H4.
source: Since CAF-1 is a monomer in complex with H3/H4, the dimerization observed for Cac1 alone is likely masked by other subunit interactions in intact CAF-1.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work and the current findings.

claim: The region required for tetramerization, between amino acids 386 and 421, overlaps the highly acidic ED domain (residues 383–436).
source: Importantly, the region required for tetramerization, between amino acids 386 and 421, overlaps the highly acidic ED domain (residues 383–436).
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation experiments.

claim: The Cac1 ED domain interacts with H3/H4.
source: Our studies reveal its role in CAF-1-induced (H3/H4)2 tetramer formation, consistent with the observation that deletion of the p150 ED domain has chromatin assembly defects (Kaufman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation experiments and supported by citation to Kaufman et al., 1995.

claim: Other histone chaperones use acidic patches/surfaces for histone binding.
source: Therefore, the Cac1 ED domain interacts with H3/H4, which is similar to how other histone chaperones use acidic patches/surfaces for histone binding (Das et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2010.

claim: The CAF-1 conformation may be significantly different with and without histones.
source: The CAF-1 conformation may be significantly different with and without histones, as evidenced by the different inter-subunit cross-linking patterns between CAF-1 and CAF-1-H3/H4 samples (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the CX-MS data showing different cross-linking patterns.

claim: Extensive changes in HX occur throughout Cac1 with H3/H4 binding, even in regions not in direct contact with H3/H4.
source: In addition, extensive changes in HX occur throughout Cac1 with H3/H4 binding, even in regions not in direct contact with H3/H4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by HX-MS data (Figure 2A).

claim: H3/H4 binding induces large structural changes in CAF-1.
source: Together, these results suggest that H3/H4 binding induces large structural changes in CAF-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the HX and CX-MS data.

claim: Passage of the replisome stalls or slows with depletion of the histone chaperones FACT, Asf1, or CAF-1 in vivo and in vitro.
source: DNA replication is coupled to histone chaperone function, as passage of the replisome stalls or slows with depletion of the histone chaperones FACT, Asf1, or CAF-1 in vivo and in vitro (Groth et al., 2007; Hoek and Stillman, 2003; Schlesinger and Formosa, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Groth et al., 2007; Hoek and Stillman, 2003; Schlesinger and Formosa, 2000).

claim: The conservative model of (H3/H4)2 tetramer inheritance during replication is an important mechanism for epigenetic inheritance of histone marks.
source: The conservative model of (H3/H4)2 tetramer inheritance during replication (Prior et al., 1980; Xu et al., 2010; Hoek and Stillman, 2003), an important mechanism for epigenetic inheritance of histone marks, is explained by the tetramer form of histones maintained by CAF-1.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Prior et al., 1980; Xu et al., 2010; Hoek and Stillman, 2003).

claim: Monomeric CAF-1 is capable of binding (H3/H4)2 tetramers through a minimal bipartite region in the monomeric Cac1 subunit.
source: In contrast to other known mechanisms, monomeric CAF-1 is capable of binding (H3/H4)2 tetramers through a minimal bipartite region in the monomeric Cac1 subunit.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing Cac1386 is sufficient for tetramerization.

claim: Mutations designed to disrupt interactions identified in this study impair the CAF-1-dependent DNA damage response in vivo.
source: The interactions identified by this study indeed appear to affect CAF-1-H3/H4 structure and function, as mutations designed to disrupt them impair the CAF-1-dependent DNA damage response in vivo (Figures 2C and 3C).
evidence: This is shown by yeast zeocin sensitivity assays (Figures 2C and 3C).
